Antigua and Barbuda.note: These Caribbean islands were a British colony until 1958.

Argentina.note: The anniversary on 10 June is still observed each year as Día de la Seguridad Vial (road safety day).

Australia.note: British colonies before 1901. Includes Australian external territories.

Austria.note: Originally LHT, like most of Austria-Hungary, but switched sides after the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany.

Bahamas.note: British colony before 1973. Caribbean island. Most passenger vehicles are LHD due to them being imported from the United States.

Bahrain.note: Former British protectorate. Switched to the same side as its neighbours. An island nation, linked by road to the Arabian mainland since 1986.

Bangladesh.note: Part of Pakistan before 1971, which was part of British India before 1947.

Barbados.note: This Atlantic island state was a British colony before 1966.

Belize.note: British colony before 1981. Switched to same side as neighbours.

Benin.note: Part of French West Africa before 1960.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.note: Switched sides after the collapse of Austria-Hungary.

Burkina Faso.note: Part of French West Africa before 1958.

Burundi.note: Belgian colony before 1962. Considering switching to LHT.

DR Congo.note: Belgian colony before 1960. RHD vehicles are common, especially in the southeast.

Croatia.note: Was then part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Cyprus.note: Under UK administration before 1960. Island nation. De facto divided between the Republic of Cyprus, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, the UN buffer zone and the British base areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia. All are LHT.

Czech Republic.note: Switched during the German occupation of Czechoslovakia.

Denmark.note: Includes the Faroe Islands and Greenland. Danish West Indies were LHT, and continue to be LHT as United States Virgin Islands after US purchase in 1917.

Dominican Republic.note: Under Spanish control until 1821 and again from 1861 to 1865.

Eswatini.note: British protectorate until 1968. Continues to drive on the same side as neighbouring countries.

Fiji.note: The island nation was a British colony before 1970.

France.note: Includes French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Saint Pierre and Miquelon, Wallis and Futuna, French Guiana, Réunion, Saint Barthélemy, the Collectivity of Saint Martin, Guadeloupe, and Mayotte.

Gambia.note: British colony until 1965. Switched to RHT on 1 October 1965 being surrounded by the former French colony of Senegal.

Georgia.note: The bus line on Ilia Chavchavadze Avenue runs on the left.

Ghana.note: British colony until 1957. Ghana switched to RHT in 1974, a Twi language slogan was "Nifa, Nifa Enan" or "Right, Right, Fourth". Ghana has also banned RHD vehicles – it prohibited new registrations of RHD vehicles after 1 August 1974, three days before the traffic change.

Gibraltar.note: Gibraltar is RHT because of its land border with Spain.

Greece.note: Originally LHT (albeit unofficially) since independence. The establishment of the traffic code switched traffic officially to RHT traffic in 1926.

Guinea.note: Part of French West Africa before 1958.

Guinea-Bissau.note: Portuguese colony until 1974. Drives on the same side as its neighbours.

Guyana.note: British colony until 1966. One of the only two countries in continental America which are in LHT, the other being Suriname.

Hungary.note: Originally LHT, like most of Austria-Hungary, but switched sides during World War II.

Iceland.note: This Atlantic island nation changed to RHT on H-dagurinn. Most passenger cars were already LHD.

Indonesia.note: Roads and railways were built by the Dutch, with LHT for roads to conform to British and Japanese standards and RHT for railways to conform with Dutch standards. Urban railways also use RHT. Did not change sides, unlike the Netherlands, in 1906.

Ireland.note: What is now the Republic of Ireland was part of the United Kingdom before 1922. The Republic covers most of the island of Ireland; the rest of Ireland is part of Northern Ireland, which remains part of the United Kingdom, which is also LHT.

Ivory Coast.note: Part of French West Africa before 1960.

Jamaica.note: British colony before 1962. Caribbean island. Most passenger vehicles are RHD, tractor-trailers and other heavy-duty trucks are mostly LHD due to being imported from the United States.

Japan.note: LHT was enacted in law in 1924. One of the few non-British-colony countries to use LHT. Okinawa Prefecture was RHT from 24 June 1945 to 30 July 1978 because of American rule.

Kenya.note: Part of the British East Africa Protectorate before 1963.

Kiribati.note: This Pacific island nation was a British colony before 1979.

Kyrgyzstan.note: In 2012, over 20,000 cheap used RHD cars were imported from Japan.

Laos.note: French protectorate until 1953. The First Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge is LHT in connection to Thailand.

Lesotho.note: British protectorate from 1885 to 1966. Enclave of LHT South Africa.

Madagascar.note: This island nation was a French colony until 1958.

Maldives.note: This island nation was a British colony before 1965.

Mali.note: Part of French West Africa before 1960.

Mauritania.note: Part of French West Africa before 1960. Mining roads between Fderîck and Zouérat are LHT.

Mauritius.note: This island nation was a British colony before 1968.

Morocco.note: Under French and Spanish protection until 1956.

Mozambique.note: Portuguese colony until 1975. Drives on the same side as its neighbours.

Myanmar.note: British colony until 1948. Switched to RHT under the orders of Ne Win. Theories emerge on the reasoning behind this switch; one claimed that he met an astrologer that recommended him to switch the country's traffic to the right in order to make the nation prosper, while another claimed that international visits caused him to notice that most countries are RHT and so decided to convert the country's handedness of traffic in order to connect Myanmar's roads with other countries' roads in the future.

Namibia.note: When South Africa occupied German South West Africa in World War I, it switched to LHT. South West Africa was administered by South Africa 1920–1990.

Nauru.note: This island nation was administered by Australia until 1968.

Nepal.note: Shares open land border with LHT India.

Netherlands.note: Includes Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten.

New Zealand.note: These Pacific islands, including territories Niue and Cook Islands, were former British colonies.

Niger.note: Part of French West Africa before 1958.

Nigeria.note: British colony until 1960. Under the military government, it switched to RHT due to being surrounded by RHT former French colonies.

North Korea.note: Was LHT during the period of Japanese rule. Switched to RHT after the Surrender of Japan.

Palau.note: Palau was under American control until 1986. Most passenger vehicles are RHD due to them being imported from Australia and Japan.

Papua New Guinea.note: After Australia occupied German New Guinea during World War I, it switched to LHT.

Philippines.note: Was LHT during the Spanish and American colonial periods. Switched to RHT after the Battle of Manila in 1945. RHD vehicles such as imported buses were still used up until the late 1980s. Philippine National Railways switched to RHT in 2010. Nowadays RHD vehicles are illegal to register and operate for ordinary use under Republic Act 8506 of 1998 however RHD vintage vehicles made before 1960 in "showroom" condition or off-road specialized vehicles are allowed to be used only for motorsports events.

Poland.note: South-eastern Poland (former Austrian Partition) was LHT until the 1920s.

Portugal.note: Colonies Goa, Macau and Mozambique, which had land borders with LHT countries, did not switch and continue to drive on the left. The Porto Metro uses RHT.

Qatar.note: Former British protectorate. Switched to same side as neighbours.

Romania.note: Regions of Romania (Transylvania, Bukovina, parts of the Banat, Crișana and Maramureș) that were part of Austria-Hungary were LHT until 1919.

Russia.note: In the Russian Far East, RHD vehicles are common due to the import of used cars from nearby Japan. The railway between Moscow and Ryazan, the Sormovskaya line in Nizhny Novgorod Metro and the Moskva River cable car use LHT.

Rwanda.note: Belgian colony before 1962. Considering switching to LHT.

Saint Kitts and Nevis.note: This Caribbean island nation was a British colony before 1983.

Saint Lucia.note: This Caribbean island nation was a British colony before 1979.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.note: This Caribbean island nation was a British colony before 1979.

Samoa.note: Despite New Zealand occupying German Samoa during the first World War, the country did not switch to LHT until 2009; this was for economic reasons, to allow cheaper importation of cars from Australia, New Zealand and Japan.

Senegal.note: Part of French West Africa before 1960.

Serbia.note: (As part of Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes). Vojvodina was LHT while part of Austria-Hungary.

Seychelles.note: This island nation was a British colony until 1976.

Sierra Leone.note: British colony until 1961. Switched to RHT being surrounded by neighbouring former French colonies. Furthermore, it banned the importation of RHD vehicles in 2013.

Singapore.note: This island nation was a British colony until 1963. It was also part of Malaysia until 1965.

Slovakia.note: Switched during the German occupation of Czechoslovakia.

Slovenia.note: (As part of Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.) Officially LHT from 1915 as part of Austria-Hungary.

Solomon Islands.note: This island nation was a British protectorate before 1975.

Somalia.note: The former British Somaliland had LHT until it formed a union with the former Italian Somaliland which had RHT.

South Korea.note: Was LHT during the period of Japanese rule. Switched to RHT after the USAMGIK Ordinance 65 came into effect.

Spain.note: Up to the 1920s Barcelona was RHT, and Madrid was LHT until 1924. The Madrid Metro still uses LHT.

Sudan.note: Formerly Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, it switched sides 17 years later to match neighbours.

Suriname.note: Dutch colony until 1975. One of the only two countries in continental America which are in LHT, the other being Guyana. Did not switch sides, unlike the Netherlands itself.

Sweden.note: The day of the switch was known as Dagen H. Most passenger vehicles were already LHD. Railways and the Stockholm Metro did not switch and continue to drive on the left.

Taiwan.note: Was LHT during the period of Japanese rule. The Republic of China (1912–1949) changed Taiwan to RHT in 1946 along with the rest of China.

Thailand.note: One of the few non-British-colony LHT countries. Shares a long land border with RHT Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia.

Timor-Leste.note: Portuguese colony until 1975. Switched to RHT with Portugal in 1928; following its annexation by Indonesia in 1976, it switched back to LHT, which it has retained since independence.

Togo.note: Part of French West Africa until 1960.

Tonga.note: British protectorate before 1970. Polynesian island nation.

Tunisia.note: RHT was enforced in the French protectorate of Tunisia from 1881 to 1956.

Turkey.note: Except Metrobus, which is usually LHT.

Tuvalu.note: Formerly a British colony. Became independent in 1978.

Uganda.note: Part of British Uganda Protectorate from 1894 until 1962.

Ukraine.note: Western parts of the country had LHT under Austro-Hungarian Empire

Uruguay.note: Became LHT in 1918, but as in some other countries in South America, changed to RHT in 1945. A speed limit of 30 km/h (19 mph) was observed until 30 September for safety.

Vanuatu.note: Co-administered under France and the United Kingdom until 1980.

Vietnam.note: French colony until 1954. The Long Bien Bridge uses LHT.

Yemen.note: South Yemen, formerly the British colony of Aden, changed to RHT in 1977, having become one of a few communist countries to use LHT. A series of postage stamps commemorating the event was issued. At that time, North Yemen was already RHT.

Zimbabwe.note: British colony before 1965 (de facto) or 1980 (de jure).

Canada.note: British Columbia: Interior changed 15 July 1920, Vancouver and the coastal area 1 January 1922; Newfoundland and Labrador: Was a British Dominion until 1949.

China.note: Parts of China were LHT in the 1930s.

Hong Kong.note: part of China; Hong Kong was a British colony from 1841 to 1941 and from 1945 to 1997, when the dependent territory was transferred to China.

Macau.note: part of China; Macau was under Portuguese rule until 1999, when the dependent territory was transferred to China.

United Kingdom.note: An island nation with a land border with the Republic of Ireland, which is also LHT. Also LHT are the British Overseas Territories of Anguilla, Ascension Island, Montserrat, Saint Helena, and Tristan da Cunha. The Heathrow airport PRT uses RHT.

Bermuda.note: part of United Kingdom; Some commercial vehicles are LHD due to imports from the United States, which has RHT.

British Indian Ocean Territory.note: part of United Kingdom; The largest island, Diego Garcia, was leased to the United States Navy as a military base; the United States is RHT.

British Virgin Islands.note: part of United Kingdom; Most passenger vehicles are LHD due to imports from the United States, which is RHT.

Cayman Islands.note: part of United Kingdom; Most passenger vehicles are LHD due to imports from the United States, which has RHT.

Falkland Islands.note: part of United Kingdom; Briefly switched to RHT during the Falklands War.

Guernsey.note: part of United Kingdom; Was RHT from 1940 to 1945 due to the German occupation.

Jersey.note: part of United Kingdom; Was RHT from 1940 to 1945 due to the German occupation.

Pitcairn Islands.note: part of United Kingdom; There is no official vehicle registration system.

South Georgia and the South Sandwich Isl.note: part of United Kingdom; Briefly switched to RHT during the Falklands War.

Turks and Caicos Islands.note: part of United Kingdom; Most passenger vehicles are LHD due to imports from the United States, which has RHT.

United States.note: British colonies before 1776 (de facto) or 1783 (de jure)

U.S. Virgin Islands.note: part of United States; U.S. Virgin Islands, like much of the Caribbean, is LHT and is the only American jurisdiction that still has LHT, because the islands drove on the left when the US purchased the former Danish West Indies in the 1917 Treaty of the Danish West Indies. Most passenger vehicles are LHD due to them being imported from the American mainland.
